What was the "Jupiter Effect", and what happened in 1982?
A 1974 book claimed a 1982 planetary alignment would trigger great earthquakes. Some prophecy writers added it to their end-time scheme. Nothing happened.

In 1974 John Gribbin and Stephen Plagemann published The Jupiter Effect. They suggested that in 1982 the planets would line up on one side of the sun. This, they said, might stir up solar activity and set off earthquakes such as on California's San Andreas Fault. In 1980 Hal Lindsey wrote that the alignment would slow the earth's spin, strain fault lines and cause floods and nuclear plant meltdowns. In March 1982 the planets were in their loose grouping. Nothing unusual happened. Gribbin himself later said he regretted the forecast. The fulfilled reading uses this case as a warning. Speculative science was joined to prophecy and presented as biblical. Scripture never mentions a planetary alignment.
In 1982 the planets were spread over nearly 100 degrees on one side of the sun, not in a straight line.
Scientists noted at the time that the tidal pull of the planets on the sun is tiny.

Most futurist scholars never endorsed the Jupiter Effect and see it as a fringe claim. They agree that prophecy should not be tied to speculative science. They argue that one teacher's mistake should not be used to judge the whole futurist reading.
Are the "terrors and great signs from heaven" in Luke 21:11 UFOs or demonic spacecraft?
The fulfilled reading says no. Luke 21:11 lists signs given before Jerusalem fell, and Josephus records omens in the sky in those very years.

In 1980 Hal Lindsey wrote that UFOs are real and that demons would stage a spacecraft landing, claiming to have planted life on earth. He linked this to Luke 21:11. The fulfilled reading notes several steps in that argument that were never proved. It quotes a sky text without checking how the Bible uses such language. It then assumes UFOs are real, that they are demons, and that the Bible predicts them. Luke 21:11 is part of the answer to the disciples' question about the temple. Josephus and Tacitus record signs in the sky before AD 70. They tell of a sword-like star, a comet, and armies seen in the clouds (Jewish War 6.5.3; Tacitus, Histories 5.13). These fit Jesus' words in their setting without any appeal to aliens.
Jewish War 6.5.3: before sunset, chariots and armed troops were seen running through the clouds.
Luke 21:12 says "before all these" the disciples would be arrested. This shows that verse 11 belongs to their own lifetime.

Most futurist scholars do not teach that UFOs fulfil prophecy, though a few writers do. Many Christians of all views agree that demonic deception will be real at the end (2 Thessalonians 2:9). Others think Luke 21:11 has both a first-century and an end-time fulfilment.
What does it mean to read Revelation "at face value"?
On the fulfilled reading, it means reading Revelation as its first readers would, as a book of symbols drawn from the Old Testament. It does not mean finding modern machines in it.

Charles Ryrie advised readers to take Revelation's beasts, horsemen and numbers "at face value". Yet he also suggested that the locusts of Revelation 9 might be "warlike UFOs". The fulfilled reading sees a contradiction here. A face-value reading should ask what John's words meant to churches in Asia in the first century. John says the book is "signified", or shown in signs (Revelation 1:1). He calls it prophecy for things that must soon happen (Revelation 1:1, 3). He explains some symbols himself: stars are angels and lampstands are churches (Revelation 1:20). If the locusts were UFOs, no Christian could have understood them for nineteen centuries. The fulfilled reading says God wrote to be understood by those first readers.
Revelation 1:20: "the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches" — John explains a symbol himself.
Revelation 17:9: the seven heads are seven mountains, and the text says so plainly.

Literal futurists say "face value" means taking events as real unless the text marks them as symbols. They say John's "like" language often describes real things he could not name. Idealists read the symbols as timeless truths about the conflict between God and evil.
Are the locusts of Revelation 9 attack helicopters?
The fulfilled reading says no. The locust picture comes from Joel 1-2, where an army is described as locusts with horses' looks and lions' teeth.

In 1973 Hal Lindsey wrote that a friend who served in Vietnam thought the locusts were Cobra helicopters, spraying nerve gas from their tails. In 1997 he expanded this. He said the crowns were pilots' helmets, the faces were pilots seen through the windscreen, the women's hair was the spinning rotor, and the teeth were a nose cannon. The fulfilled reading says this is the opposite of literal reading. It turns hair into a propeller. It also ignores the source. In Joel, a locust plague and an invading army merge. They have teeth like a lion (Joel 1:6), look like horses (Joel 2:4), and sound like chariots (Joel 2:5). John borrows Joel's picture of a judging army. He does not describe machines from the future.
Joel 2:4-5: "Their appearance is like the appearance of horses ... like the noise of chariots."
Revelation 9:5 limits the torment to five months, which is about the life span of a locust.

Some popular futurists still suggest modern weapons. Most futurist scholars, such as Robert Thomas, read the locusts as demonic beings from the abyss, not machines. Historicists linked them to the Arab armies of the 600s. Idealists read them as spiritual torment for those without God's seal.
Why do Revelation's opening words, "must soon take place" and "the time is near", matter?
They set the time frame for the whole book. On the fulfilled reading, a book meant for events "soon" cannot be a hidden code for the twenty-first century.

Revelation begins by saying it shows things that "must soon take place" (Revelation 1:1). It blesses those who read and keep it "for the time is near" (Revelation 1:3). It ends the same way: "the time is near" and "I am coming soon" (Revelation 22:6, 10, 12). Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far off (Daniel 12:4). John is told not to seal his, because its time is near (Revelation 22:10). The fulfilled reading says that some popular readers focus on hidden symbols but pass over these plain time words. They then say John saw helicopters he could not understand. This reading says the plain time markers should guide how we read the symbols, not the other way round.
Daniel 12:4 ("seal the book until the time of the end") is contrasted with Revelation 22:10 ("do not seal").
The letters to seven real churches in Revelation 2-3 address problems in their own day.

Futurists say "soon" can mean "suddenly" or reflect God's view of time (2 Peter 3:8). Idealists say the events are always near because they recur in every age. Many scholars hold that the book had meaning for its first readers and also looks to the final return.
Why do popular prophecy readings change with the times?
Because they tie the text to current technology and politics. When the headlines change, the reading changes too.

Lindsey's Vietnam-era friend saw Cobra helicopters in Revelation 9. A later version of the same reading dropped Vietnam and spoke of modern attack helicopters. In the 1970s, the Soviet Union was the northern invader. After 1991 other nations took the role. In 1977 Iran was the rising power. Later Iraq became the focus. The fulfilled reading says this is a sign the method is wrong. A true reading of Scripture should give the same meaning to its first readers and to us. The Bible warns against being "tossed by every wind" (Ephesians 4:14). A reading that can apply equally to medieval cavalry or modern aircraft does not explain the text. It only reflects the reader's own time.
The same locust text was read as cavalry by medieval readers and as aircraft by modern ones.
Readings of Ezekiel 38 moved from Russia to other nations after the Soviet Union fell in 1991.

Futurists reply that the meaning of prophecy stays the same even if application changes. They say teachers can be wrong in detail while the overall scheme stands. They also note that fulfilled readers sometimes change their own identifications, for example about who the beast was.
What basic question should we ask when the Bible describes falling heavenly bodies?
We should ask how the Bible itself uses this language. Comparing Scripture with Scripture shows that it is a familiar way of picturing the fall of rulers and nations.

The fulfilled reading proposes a simple rule. Let the Bible interpret itself. Before guessing about asteroids or UFOs, ask where else the Old Testament speaks of darkened suns and falling stars. The answer is clear. Isaiah uses it for Babylon (Isaiah 13:10) and Edom (Isaiah 34:4). Ezekiel uses it for Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7-8). Amos uses it for Israel (Amos 8:9). Joel uses it for Judah (Joel 2:10). In each case a real nation falls in history, and the sky language shows that God is the judge. The earth goes on, and the stars still shine. Jesus also set a time limit: all these things within "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). The next chapter of this study works through these texts in detail.
Isaiah 13:10 and Matthew 24:29 use almost the same words about sun, moon and stars.
Peter says Joel's darkened sun and blood moon were "what was spoken" in his own day at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-20).

Futurists agree the language is used figuratively in the Old Testament. They argue that at Christ's final return it may also be literal, since the whole creation will be renewed (Romans 8:21; 2 Peter 3:10). Many scholars see both: figurative judgments in history point to a final cosmic renewal.
Did Jesus tell Christians in every age to watch the skies for signs?
On the fulfilled reading, the signs in Luke 21:25 were for his own disciples. They were to watch for Jerusalem's fall, which would happen within "this generation".

Some teachers cite Luke 21:25 as an instruction to look to the skies. But the verse sits inside a passage about Jerusalem being surrounded and trampled (Luke 21:20-24). Jesus then says, "when these things begin to happen, look up ... your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:28). He compares this to a fig tree showing that summer is near (Luke 21:29-31). Then he says, "this generation will not pass away until all things take place" (Luke 21:32). The fulfilled reading says that the people told to "look up" are the same people who would see the armies. Their "redemption" was rescue from the persecutors and the end of the old order. That fits the time words better than a call to all later generations to study the sky.
Luke 21:28: "look up and lift up your heads" is addressed to "you", the disciples.
Luke 21:32 sets a limit of "this generation" for "all things".

Futurists see Luke 21:25-28 as a move from AD 70 (verses 20-24) to the end of the age after "the times of the Gentiles". They hold that redemption here means the final resurrection. Many scholars think Luke separates the two events more clearly than Matthew.
What does "immediately after the tribulation of those days" tell us about the timing of Matthew 24:29?
It ties the darkened sun and falling stars directly to the tribulation just described. On the fulfilled reading, there is no room for a gap of 2,000 years.

Matthew 24:29 begins, "Immediately after the tribulation of those days". The tribulation is the one in verses 15-28: the flight from Judea and the siege. Matthew uses the Greek word for "immediately" for actions that follow at once. Jesus came up from the water immediately (Matthew 3:16). The fishermen left their nets immediately (Matthew 4:20, 22). The rooster crowed immediately (Matthew 26:74). The fulfilled reading says the word should mean the same here. Whatever verse 29 describes, it follows straight after Jerusalem's tribulation. Verse 34 then adds that "all these things" would happen within "this generation". A reading that puts verse 29 thousands of years after verse 28 must stretch "immediately" beyond its normal sense.
Matthew 26:74: Peter denies Jesus, and "immediately the rooster crowed".
Matthew 14:31: "immediately Jesus stretched out his hand" to catch the sinking Peter.

Futurists answer that "those days" refers to a future tribulation, so "immediately" follows that future event, not AD 70. Others suggest "immediately" works from God's view of time, or that it means "suddenly". Some evangelical scholars see verse 29 as following the whole age of distress that began in AD 70.
How do the early signs and the later signs in the discourse fit together?
The early signs (wars, famines, earthquakes) are only "the beginning of birth pains". The later signs come near the end, when the city and temple are about to fall.

Jesus said that wars and rumours of wars must happen, "but the end is not yet" (Matthew 24:6). Luke adds that "the end will not follow immediately" (Luke 21:9). These early troubles are "the beginning of birth pains" (Matthew 24:8). They covered the years after the ascension. Then come the decisive signs: armies around Jerusalem, the abomination, the flight and the great distress (Matthew 24:15-28). After that, "immediately", comes the collapse pictured by the darkened sun and falling stars (Matthew 24:29). On the fulfilled reading, this is a timeline within one generation. It moves from early warnings, to the war, to the fall of the Jewish state. That state had seemed as fixed as the stars.
Luke 21:9: "these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once".
Luke 21:12: "before all these things" the disciples would be persecuted, which Acts records.

Futurists agree there is a sequence but place the later signs in a future tribulation. Many amillennial scholars see the birth pains as the whole church age. Some evangelical scholars see the sequence move from AD 70 to the end of history, with the timing left open.
Should we expect the sun to go literally dark and the stars to fall from the sky?
The fulfilled reading says no. Jesus used standard prophetic language for the fall of a nation, and the disciples had not asked about the end of the physical world.

God can darken the sun if he wills. The question is what Jesus meant. The disciples asked about the temple and "the end of the age" (Matthew 24:3). The word is "age" (aion), not the physical world (kosmos). Jesus answered in the language of the prophets. Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos and Joel all spoke of a dark sun, a moon without light and falling stars when a nation came under judgment. These words describe real events in history: Babylon's fall, Egypt's defeat, Israel's exile. In each case the heavens stayed in place. Even many futurist writers do not say that Matthew 24:29-31 describes the end of the physical universe. On the fulfilled reading, verse 29 means that Israel's ruling order was about to collapse.
Isaiah 13:10 uses this language for Babylon's fall to the Medes in 539 BC. The sun still rose the next day.
Matthew 24:3 asks about "the end of the age", the same phrase used in Matthew 13:39-40.

Futurists answer that at Christ's final return, real cosmic signs will occur. They cite Revelation 6:12-14 and 2 Peter 3:10. They grant that the language was figurative in the Old Testament but argue that its final use may be literal. Many scholars hold both: figurative in history, with full cosmic renewal at the end.
How can stars fall to the earth and the earth survive (Revelation 6:13; 12:4)?
Read literally, it cannot. Even one star is far bigger than the earth. This shows the language is symbolic.

Revelation 6:13 says the stars fell to the earth like figs from a tree. Revelation 12:4 says the dragon's tail swept a third of the stars and threw them to earth. A star like our sun is more than a hundred times wider than the earth. One star coming near would destroy the planet. Some literalist writers, such as E. W. Bullinger, insisted that these texts must be taken literally. But the text then goes on to describe life continuing on earth. Revelation 12 itself explains its symbols: the dragon is Satan (Revelation 12:9). The fulfilled reading says the stars are also symbols. They stand for powers or rulers, as in Daniel 8:10, where a horn casts down some of the host and stars.
Daniel 8:10: a horn grows up to the host of heaven and throws some of the stars to the ground. This is Antiochus attacking God's people.
Revelation 1:20: John himself says "the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches".

Some futurists take "stars" here as meteors or as fallen angels. Most scholars of all views agree that Revelation 12:4 is symbolic, often of angels who followed Satan. Futurists still read Revelation 6:12-14 as real cosmic upheaval at the end.
Could the "stars" in these passages be meteorites?
That reading leaves literalism behind and still meets the same problem. A third of heaven's meteorites striking earth would end all life.

Some interpreters, such as John Walvoord, suggested the falling stars could be meteorites. The fulfilled reading makes three points. First, calling stars "meteorites" is already a non-literal reading, the very thing literalists object to. Second, if it is meteorites in Revelation 6:13 and 12:4, it must be meteorites in Matthew 24:29 too. Third, the damage would be enormous. Scientists think one asteroid about 10 kilometres wide struck Mexico 66 million years ago and caused a mass extinction. A shower of such objects would leave no world for a millennium. The fulfilled reading concludes that the better path is to read the stars as the Bible itself does: as rulers and powers.
The Chicxulub impact released energy estimated at about 100 million megatons.
Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9) shows stars standing for persons, not rocks.

Futurists answer that God can preserve life through great disasters, and that "star" in ancient speech could include any light in the sky, including meteors. Some take the stars as angels or demons. Others hold the language is partly figurative but points to real physical upheaval.
Where does the Bible use stars to represent people or nations?
From Abraham onward. God promised Abraham descendants like the stars, and later texts use stars for Israel, its rulers and the righteous.

God told Abraham to count the stars and said, "so shall your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5; 22:17; 26:4). Moses told Israel they had become as many as the stars (Deuteronomy 1:10). Balaam foretold that "a star shall come out of Jacob", a ruler from Israel (Numbers 24:17). Daniel says the wise will shine "like the stars" (Daniel 12:3). Jude calls false teachers "wandering stars" (Jude 13). Even today we call a famous person a "rising star" and say a disgraced leader's star has fallen. Many national flags carry stars, suns and moons as signs of their nation. The fulfilled reading says this is why Jesus could use falling stars for Israel's rulers without being misunderstood by his hearers.
Numbers 24:17: "a star shall come out of Jacob, a scepter shall rise out of Israel" — the star is a king.
The flags of the United States, China and Brazil use stars for states, peoples or regions.

Most scholars agree that stars often stand for people in Scripture. Futurists respond that this does not settle Matthew 24:29, since the context there may describe real signs in the sky. Some note that stars also stand for angels (Job 38:7; Revelation 1:20).
Why does the Bible link the sun, moon and stars with rulers?
Because from the start God made the lights to "rule" the day and night. Joseph's dream then used sun, moon and stars for his parents and brothers.

In Genesis 1:16-18, God made the greater light "to rule the day" and the lesser light "to rule the night". The heavenly lights are pictured as rulers from the beginning. In Joseph's second dream, the sun, moon and eleven stars bowed to him (Genesis 37:9). Jacob understood at once: "Shall I and your mother and your brothers bow down to you?" (Genesis 37:10). No one thought the real sun would bow. At seventeen, Joseph lived under the authority of his family. The dream foretold that he would one day rule over them, which happened in Egypt (Genesis 42:6). The fulfilled reading says this sets the pattern. In Scripture's picture-language, sun, moon and stars stand for a ruling house and its people.
Genesis 37:10: Jacob rebukes Joseph, but he understands the dream at once as being about his family.
Genesis 42:6: Joseph's brothers bow down before him with their faces to the ground.

Most commentators of all views agree on the meaning of Joseph's dream. Even dispensational writers note that the sun, moon and stars there stand for rulers and for Israel. Futurists accept the symbolism in Genesis but argue that Matthew 24:29 may still describe literal signs.
What does it mean that "the stars fought from heaven" in Judges 5:20?
It is poetic parallelism. "Kings came and fought" in verse 19 and "the stars fought" in verse 20 describe the same battle.

The Song of Deborah celebrates Israel's victory over Sisera. Verse 19 says, "The kings came and fought". Verse 20 says, "From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera". Hebrew poetry often says the same thing twice in different words. Here the stars are kings and armies seen in heavenly terms. They may also point to God's heavenly host fighting for Israel. A storm also swept the enemy away at the river Kishon (Judges 5:21). No one reads this to mean that stars left their places and fought. The fulfilled reading uses this as a simple test. If literal-minded readers accept poetic stars here, they should allow the same in Matthew 24:29.
Judges 5:19-20: "kings came and fought" is paired with "the stars fought from heaven".
Judges 4:15 tells the same battle in prose: "the Lord routed Sisera".

Most scholars agree this is poetry. Some see a reference to a storm or to angelic armies rather than kings. Futurists accept figurative language in poetry but note that Matthew 24 is prophecy in a discourse, which they think may be more literal.
Who is the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and twelve stars on her head (Revelation 12:1)?
She draws on Joseph's dream and stands for the people of God, Israel in her glory, who brought forth the Messiah.

John sees a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars. She is in labour and gives birth to a son who will rule the nations (Revelation 12:1-5). The sun, moon and twelve stars echo Joseph's dream (Genesis 37:9), where they stand for Jacob's family. The twelve stars match the twelve tribes. Many commentators, including some who call themselves literalists, read her as Israel or the faithful people of God. Some add that she continues as the church. Isaiah pictures Zion as a mother in labour (Isaiah 66:7-8). The fulfilled reading sees a contrast. In Revelation 12 Israel shines in glory as she brings forth the Messiah. In Matthew 24:29 the same lights go dark as the nation that rejected him falls.
Isaiah 66:7-8: Zion gives birth to a son before her labour pains came.
Revelation 17 shows a different woman, the harlot. Many contrast her with the faithful woman of chapter 12.

Roman Catholic tradition often sees Mary as the woman. Dispensationalists usually see national Israel, who will be protected in a future tribulation (Revelation 12:6). Many Protestant scholars read the woman as the one people of God, Israel and the church together.
Did older Bible commentators read Matthew 24:29 as the fall of the Jewish state?
Many did. Writers such as John Lightfoot, John Gill, Adam Clarke and Thomas Newton read the darkened sun and falling stars as the end of Israel's religious and civil order.

This reading is not new. In the 1600s John Lightfoot read Matthew 24 in light of Jerusalem's fall. Thomas Newton's work on prophecy (1754) said that great changes on earth are often shown in prophecy as changes in the heavens. John Gill and Adam Clarke read verse 29 the same way. Clarke wrote that the sun stood for the religion of the Jewish church, the moon for its state, and the stars for its judges and teachers. Older writers sometimes cited Josephus' report that the Zealots killed about 12,000 of the city's leading men (Jewish War 4.6.1). On this reading, the "stars" truly fell. The fulfilled reading claims that this view was common before modern speculative schemes became popular.
Adam Clarke on Matthew 24:29: the Jewish "heaven" perishes and its sun and moon are darkened.
Jewish War 4.6.1: Josephus reports 12,000 of the nobility killed by the Zealots.

Many older commentators, such as Matthew Henry, saw verse 29 as having a double meaning, both AD 70 and the end of the world. Futurists note that the church fathers mostly read verses 29-31 as Christ's final return. Some scholars think the older Protestant view was shaped by debates of its own time.
How does Isaiah 13 help explain Matthew 24:29?
Isaiah 13 uses nearly the same words—dark sun, dark moon, stars without light—for Babylon's fall to the Medes. Jesus applies that language to Jerusalem.

Isaiah 13 is "the oracle concerning Babylon" (Isaiah 13:1). It warns that "the day of the Lord is near" (Isaiah 13:6). It says the stars will not give their light, the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shine (Isaiah 13:10). It adds that the heavens will tremble and the earth shake (Isaiah 13:13). Then God names his agent: "I am stirring up the Medes" (Isaiah 13:17). This was fulfilled when the Medes and Persians took Babylon in 539 BC. Even the dispensational commentator John Martin wrote that verse 10 may figuratively describe a total change in the political order. The fulfilled reading says that if the language is figurative for Babylon, it should be figurative for Jerusalem too. Revelation later calls the persecuting city "Babylon" (Revelation 14:8).
Isaiah 13:17-19: the Medes overthrow Babylon "as when God overthrew Sodom".
Babylon fell to Cyrus' army in October 539 BC. The sun and stars were unchanged.

Futurists often say Isaiah 13 has a near fulfilment in 539 BC and a far one in the final day of the Lord. They point to verse 11, where God punishes "the world". Many scholars hold that the figurative pattern is clear but that Jesus may extend it to the final judgment. Most futurists identify Babylon in Revelation as Rome or a future world system, not Jerusalem.
What do the judgments on Egypt (Ezekiel 32) and Edom (Isaiah 34) add?
They show the same sky language used for two more nations. Egypt's lights go out when Babylon defeats it, and Edom's heavens roll up like a scroll.

Ezekiel 32:7-8 is addressed to Pharaoh. God says that when he puts him out, he will cover the heavens, darken the stars, cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon will not give its light. The agent is named: the sword of the king of Babylon (Ezekiel 32:11). Isaiah 34:4-5 says the host of heaven will rot and the sky roll up like a scroll. The stars fall like leaves, and God's sword comes down on Edom. Edom was later overrun and its people driven out of their land. No sword fell from the sky, and the heavens did not roll up. The fulfilled reading notes that Revelation 6:13-14 borrows Isaiah 34:4 almost word for word. Revelation also calls Jerusalem "Egypt" (Revelation 11:8).
Ezekiel 32:11: "The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you".
Revelation 6:14: "the sky vanished like a scroll that is rolled up" echoes Isaiah 34:4.

Futurists agree these texts are figurative judgments on Egypt and Edom. They hold that Isaiah 34 also looks ahead to a final judgment on all nations (Isaiah 34:2). Many scholars see Edom as a type of the world opposing God. They read Revelation 6 as the last day, not AD 70.
Did the prophets ever use this sky language for Israel itself?
Yes. Amos warned that the day of the Lord would be darkness for Israel, and that God would make the sun go down at noon.

Amos condemned Israel's empty worship. God said he hated their feasts and would not accept their offerings (Amos 5:21-22). Then he warned those who longed for the day of the Lord: "It is darkness, and not light" (Amos 5:18). In Amos 8:9 God says, "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight". This was fulfilled when Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Joel used similar words for an invasion of Judah (Joel 2:10). The fulfilled reading says this answers an objection. Sky language was not only used for pagan nations. God used it for his own people when they broke the covenant. Matthew 24:29 does the same for first-century Jerusalem.
Amos 8:9-10: the sun sets at noon, and feasts turn to mourning — Israel's fall to Assyria.
Joel 2:10: the earth quakes, the sun and moon are dark, as an army invades Judah.

Some read Amos 8:9 as a real solar eclipse; one occurred over the region in 763 BC. Futurists accept the historical sense but see these texts as patterns for the final day of the Lord. Most scholars agree that the day of the Lord can mean a judgment in history.
Does the New Testament ever apply cosmic language to events of its own time?
Yes. At Pentecost Peter said Joel's prophecy of a dark sun and a blood moon was "what was spoken" being fulfilled that very day.

On the day of Pentecost Peter quoted Joel 2:28-32. He said, "this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16). The quote includes wonders in the sky, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great day of the Lord (Acts 2:19-20). Peter did not wait for an eclipse. He applied the whole passage to the outpouring of the Spirit and the coming judgment on "this crooked generation" (Acts 2:40). Scholars such as R. T. France have noted that cosmic images in the Old Testament point to God's action in history. Jesus also spoke of seeing Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). The fulfilled reading says this confirms that apostles used sky language for events in their own day.
Acts 2:16-20: Peter says Joel's sun, moon and blood are "this" — what the crowd is seeing.
Acts 2:40: "Save yourselves from this crooked generation" links the prophecy to coming judgment.
